text: Lesson 29 left WKSTN-FIN-14 isolated and Teresa Marsh's account disabled, with a forensic triage capture already sitting in evidence. This lesson covers eradication, recovery, and the after-action report — finding the actual persistence mechanism, deciding whether to trust the host again, validating it before production, and writing down concrete, owned follow-up work instead of a narrative.

Monday morning, the forensic triage capture reveals root cause: a scheduled task named MicrosoftEdgeUpdateTaskMachineUA, created two minutes after Friday's foreign sign-in, built to relaunch a remote-access tool on every startup. Disguised to blend into Windows' real update tasks, it would have sat there, live, if anyone had skipped straight to re-enabling the account.

A query against DeviceProcessEvents, filtered to this host and to schtasks.exe, surfaces the exact command line that created the malicious task — the kind of specific, host-scoped forensic query this whole course has built toward since Chapter 3's detection work.

Removing the task itself is trivial; trusting the host afterward is not. SYSTEM-level persistence this disguised means the attacker had enough access that something else might still be hiding, unseen by the triage capture. So the team restores WKSTN-FIN-14 from Thursday night's backup — a full day before the compromise — and verifies its hashes against the known-good gold image before trusting it again.

Validation runs three checks before the laptop returns to Teresa: a clean Defender scan, a scheduled-task list matching baseline, and the same forensic query re-run tenant-wide to confirm nothing else carries the same indicators. The after-action report pairs each finding — push-fatigue MFA, an alert-only rule, unlogged scheduled tasks, stale training — with an owner and a due date.

Eradication, recovery, and a report with real, owned follow-up work close Teresa's incident cleanly and defensibly. But closing one report doesn't mean the broader campaign behind it is over — Lesson 31 turns this incident's own root cause into a hypothesis for a hunt that finds what this specific alert never caught.
